title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1RC0RA_1LD1RE_1LE0LE_0RA0LD_0RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1RC0RA_1LD1RE_1LE0LE_0RA0LD_0RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. Its tape is a long alternating stretch (10)^n holding a single marker 0, followed by a short, changing tail at the right end that behaves like a counter in base 3. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 10,000 steps by the kernel alone and in the first 107 with native_decide; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 109 steps; an exact macro simulator (blocks of 2 cells) finds no halt in the first 1015 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 4,585 cells have been visited and 2,285 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/power
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.309). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.349).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>15</sup> steps
claims.text: An exact macro simulator (blocks of 2 cells) runs 1015 steps without a halt. The macro simulator cuts the tape into blocks of K cells, run-length codes them, and crosses a whole run at once when the head leaves it on the far side in the state it entered with; it agrees with the plain simulator tools/c/tmrun cell for cell.

claims.title: A marker counted in base 3
claims.text: At the moments the head first reaches a new cell on the right, the tape is 0 (10)^x 0 (10)^y followed by a short tail; between consecutive such moments in one round, x grew by 243 (79 times), 81 (67 times), 27 (31 times), 9 (6 times), 729 (3 times) and a few other amounts in the first 108 steps, with 215 resets. Read as: one marker step per sweep, and a base-3 counter in the tail that gains a digit at powers of 3.

claims.title: The halting state, seen from the run
claims.text: In the first 10<sup>8</sup> steps state F was entered 75,302 times, always reading a 0 (F1 halts); 74,846 of those times the head was at least 7 cells from both ends of the visited tape.

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.26×10<sup>9</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 5.26×109 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 5 checkpoints, the last at 3.00×109 steps. No trip-level jump was used in this run, only the shift rules over repeated words (exact by induction, but the program is not verified).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. A marker 0 drifts through a long alternating sea one cell per sweep while a base-3 counter at the right end counts the sweeps; when the marker reaches the far end a reset sweep starts the next round, one cell wider.

facts.text: No halt in an exact macro simulator (blocks of 2 cells).
The marker moves 27, 81, 243, 729 cells between right growths: a ternary sweep counter.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
No halt in the C simulator; 4,585 cells visited.
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 3.00×10<sup>9</sup> steps).

sections.heading: What the machine does
html: Stop the machine whenever its head first reaches a new cell on the right. With a for 10 and c for 1110, the tape around step 5.7·107:

• step 56,958,976: 0 a^18 0 a^810 c a^3 c a^13 c a^5 1 a 1^2 C>0
  • step 57,210,619: 0 a^99 0 a^729 c a^3 c a^13 c a^5 c a c 1^2 C>0
  • step 57,808,047: 0 a^342 0 a^486 c a^3 c a^13 c a^5 c a c^2 1^2 C>0
  • step 58,297,046: E>0 a^850 0^2 a^9 0^5 … (the reset sweep)
  • step 58,315,798: 0 a^6 0 a^843 c a^8 c^3 a 1^2 C>0

The left part is an alternating sea 0 a^x 0 a^y with x + y fixed within a round (828 here, then 849): a single extra 0, the marker, sits after x copies of 10. The head shuttles between the marker and the right end; each round trip moves the marker one cell on and also updates the tail at the right end. Watching one round trip after another, the tail reads 0^2 a^4 0^2 a^14 0^2 a^6 0^2 a^2 0^2 a 0 1, then 0 1 a^4 …, then 0 a 0 a^3 …, then 0^2 a^4 0 1 a^14 …: the separators between the blocks take three forms and change like the digits of a number in base 3. The tail is a counter: the tape grows on the right only when the counter gains a digit, and between consecutive right growths the marker moves by 27, 81, 243 or 729 cells. In the first 108 steps the marker moved by 243 (79 times), 81 (67 times), 27 (31 times), 9, 729 and a few other amounts: powers of 3, so the tail counts sweeps in base 3.

When the marker reaches the right end of the sea the head makes one long sweep (E>0 a^850 …), the marker restarts near the left end and the sea is one cell longer. A round of a sea of width w is about w sweeps of w steps each, and the sea grows by one per round: the width grows like the cube root of the step count.
The near-duplicate 1RB0RE_1LC1RD_1LD0LD_0RE0LC_1RA1RF_0RA--- does the same: its marker also advances by powers of 3 (81, 243, 27, …) between right growths.

sections.heading: Where a halt would have to come from
html: The halting transition is F reading a 1. F is entered only from E reading a 1 (1RF), so a halt needs E on a 1 with another 1 just right of it. In the first 108 steps F was entered 75,302 times, every time on a 0, and 74,846 of those times at least 7 cells from both ends of the tape: the dangerous pattern would have to appear in the middle of the tape, in the sea or the counter, during a sweep.

Nothing here decides whether it can: the counter's digits at each reset depend on how many sweeps the round took, which depends on the width of the sea, so the tail's contents form a slowly varying, irregular sequence.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.309). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.349).
After 109 steps the tape spans 4,585 cells (258 left of the start, 3,474 right), with a density of 1s of 0.498.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.
